newsitem.title: UK: Odds favour one pct UK income tax cut - William Hill.
newsitem.headline: Odds favour one pct UK income tax cut - William Hill.

text.p: British bookmaker William Hill is tipping a one penny reduction in the basic rate of UK income tax at Tuesday's budget, and is offering short odds on it.

Britain is known as a nation of gamblers and the annual budget is too good an opportunity to miss. Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will stand up in parliament to deliver the 1997/98 budget at around 1530 GMT on Tuesday.

William Hill said it was offering very short odds of five-to-one on for a one penny income tax cut, taking the basic rate to 23 percent. That means a five pounds bet would yield only a six pounds return including the stake.
The bookmaker is offering three-to-one against for a two pence cut in the basic rate. In that case, a winning five pound bet would net 15 pounds.

The betting opportunities do not end there. William Hill is offering wagers on possible abolition of house purchase stamp duty, inheritance tax and even the introduction of a minimum wage, something the government opposes vehemently.

The longest odds -- 1,000-to-one against -- are offered on the reintroduction of the poll tax, the deeply unpopular charge that sparked protest riots in London in 1990 and was subsequently abolished by Prime Minister John Major.
An increase in income tax, politically unthinkable with an election six months away, is offered at 200 to one against.
Lastly, the British punter can even bet on the length of Clarke's speech. The bookmaker thinks the most likely duration is between 71 and 75 minutes.

Last year, Clarke talked for 70 minutes. The shortest British budget speech ever, at 45 minutes, was delivered by Benjamin Disraeli in 1867. Eleven years before that, William Gladstone put the House of Commons through a speech of four hours and 45 minutes, the longest ever.
